title: 3-Read Friday #53: Ofsted, Coaching, and Cognitive Load
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the fifty-third edition, Craig Barton curates posts on school inspection, coaching, and research critique. He recommends Pete Foster's recurring series analysing Ofsted reports for themes in what schools are asked to improve, calling himself a fan of the series. He then highlights Sarah Cottingham's post on closing the 'knowing-deciding-doing' gap in coaching, singling out the embedded video as worth watching. Finally, he points to Dylan Kane's critique of the 'expertise reversal effect', a piece he frames as being for 'research geeks like me', engaging with Kane's concern about loosely defined terms like expert, novice, and problem-solving in cognitive load research. Reader comments on the issue show real engagement, including one from a commenter praising the newsletter's consistent usefulness and brevity.
points: Barton flags Foster's Ofsted series as a running favourite, valuing its pattern-spotting across many inspection reports rather than a one-off take on a single school.

He singles out the embedded coaching video in Cottingham's post as adding practical value beyond the prose, hinting at his general preference for concrete classroom/coaching footage over abstract theory.
He explicitly labels the Dylan Kane pick as niche ('research geeks like me'), acknowledging that not every recommendation is meant for a broad teacher audience.

The reader comments quoted alongside the issue -- praising its brevity and breadth -- reinforce that the newsletter's own value proposition is curation under time pressure, not just the links themselves.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
This latest instalment dives deep into recent Ofsted reports to find themes and trends in what schools are asked to improve.
Another banger from Sarah, this time looking at how coaches can support teachers to close the gap between knowing what to do and actually doing it.
Dylan delves into cognitive load theory research and raises concerns about the use of terms like expert, novice, and problem-solving.
I love 3read Friday. It's relevant, useful, doesn't take more than 15mins to read, and encompasses a variety of topics that I'd never find by myself.
